statement: Let $X_1, X_2, \dots$ be pairwise [independent](c:independence), [identically distributed](c:ident-distrib) real [random variables](c:random-variable) with $E|X_1| < \infty$. Then the sample means $(X_1 + \dots + X_n)/n$ converge [almost surely](c:almost-sure-convergence) to the [expected value](c:expected-value) $E[X_1]$.
conclusion: With probability one, $\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i \to E[X_1]$ as $n \to \infty$.

formal.difference: The declaration allows values in a real Banach space and an arbitrary measure; it first treats the case $X_1 = 0$ almost everywhere and otherwise derives that the measure is a probability measure. For real variables on a probability space it states the same convergence.

proofs.name: Etemadi truncation
proofs.slogan: Truncate the variables, control the variances along a geometric subsequence, and fill the gaps between its indices by monotonicity.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, first for nonnegative variables and then for $X_i = X_i^+ - X_i^-$. The weak law follows, because almost sure convergence implies [convergence in probability](c:convergence-in-probability).

roles.why: Integrability bounds $\sum_i P(X_1 > i)$ and $\sum_i E[Y_i^2]/i^2$ by multiples of $E[X_1]$.
Pairwise independence makes the variance of a sum equal to the sum of the variances.
Identical distribution gives $P(X_i > i) = P(X_1 > i)$ and the same truncation bounds for every $i$.

steps.slogan: Split each variable into its positive part and its negative part.
steps.detail: Write $X_i = X_i^+ - X_i^-$. Each family $(X_i^{+})$ and $(X_i^{-})$ is again pairwise [independent](c:independence), identically distributed and integrable, so it suffices to prove the theorem for $X_i \ge 0$.

steps.slogan: Truncate the $i$-th variable at level $i$ and compare it with the original variable.
steps.detail: Let $Y_i = X_i \mathbf{1}\{X_i \le i\}$. Then $\sum_i P(X_i \ne Y_i) = \sum_i P(X_1 > i) \le E[X_1] < \infty$, so almost surely $X_i = Y_i$ for all large $i$. Monotone convergence gives $E[Y_i] \to E[X_1]$.

steps.slogan: Bound the variances of the truncated sums along the indices $k_n = \lfloor c^n \rfloor$.
steps.detail: Fix $c > 1$ and let $T_k = Y_1 + \dots + Y_k$. Pairwise independence gives $\operatorname{Var} T_k = \sum_{i \le k} \operatorname{Var} Y_i \le \sum_{i \le k} E[Y_i^2]$, and a geometric sum estimate gives $\sum_n \operatorname{Var}(T_{k_n})/k_n^2 \le C \sum_i E[Y_i^2]/i^2 \le C' E[X_1] < \infty$. This [variance](c:variance) bound is the core estimate.

steps.slogan: Prove convergence along the geometric subsequence with Chebyshev's inequality and the Borel–Cantelli lemma.
steps.detail: For $\varepsilon > 0$, Chebyshev's inequality gives $\sum_n P(|T_{k_n} - E T_{k_n}| > \varepsilon k_n) \le \varepsilon^{-2} \sum_n \operatorname{Var}(T_{k_n})/k_n^2 < \infty$. Borel–Cantelli and the Cesàro limit $E[T_k]/k \to E[X_1]$ give $T_{k_n}/k_n \to E[X_1]$ almost surely.

steps.slogan: Squeeze the full sequence between consecutive geometric indices by monotonicity.
steps.detail: Because $Y_i \ge 0$, $T_m$ increases with $m$. For $k_n \le m \le k_{n+1}$, $T_{k_n}/k_{n+1} \le T_m/m \le T_{k_{n+1}}/k_n$, and $k_{n+1}/k_n \to c$, so almost surely $E[X_1]/c \le \liminf T_m/m \le \limsup T_m/m \le c\,E[X_1]$.

steps.slogan: Let $c$ decrease to $1$ and return to the original variables.
steps.detail: Take $c = 1 + 1/j$ for $j = 1, 2, \dots$; the countable intersection of these events gives $T_m/m \to E[X_1]$ [almost surely](c:almost-sure-convergence). Since $X_i = Y_i$ for all large $i$, the two partial sums differ by a fixed amount, so $\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i \le n} X_i \to E[X_1]$.

concepts.c:independence: Pairwise independence is the only independence the variance bound needs.
concepts.c:ident-distrib: Identical distribution makes every truncation bound depend on $X_1$ only.
concepts.c:random-variable: The sample means are random variables whose limit the theorem controls.
concepts.c:almost-sure-convergence: The conclusion holds outside one event of probability zero.
concepts.c:expected-value: The expected value $E[X_1]$ is the limit of the sample means.
concepts.c:integrable-function: Integrability makes the truncation errors summable.
concepts.c:convergence-in-probability: The weak law is the weaker mode of convergence that follows.
concepts.c:variance: Variance bounds feed Chebyshev's inequality along the subsequence.

statement: If $f\colon A \to B$ is a map between [finite sets](c:finite-set) and $|A| > |B|$, then two different elements of $A$ have the same image; that is, $f$ is not an [injection](c:injection).
conclusion: There are $a \ne a'$ in $A$ with $f(a) = f(a')$.

formal.difference: The declaration states that two subsets $t, u$ of a finite set $s$ with $|s| < |t| + |u|$ meet. The map form is the separate declaration Fintype.exists_ne_map_eq_of_card_lt.

proofs.name: Contrapositive count
proofs.slogan: Assume that the map is injective, count its image exactly, and compare the image with the target set.
proofs.scope: The whole principle. If $B = \emptyset$ and $A \ne \emptyset$, no map $A \to B$ exists and the statement is vacuous.

roles.why: Finiteness makes $|A|$ and $|B|$ natural numbers, and a subset of a finite set has at most as many elements.
The inequality $|A| > |B|$ contradicts the bound $|A| \le |B|$ that an injective map gives.

steps.slogan: Assume that $f$ is injective, to prove the contrapositive $|A| \le |B|$.
steps.detail: The contrapositive of the principle says: if $f$ is an [injection](c:injection), then $|A| \le |B|$. So assume that $f(a) = f(a')$ implies $a = a'$.

steps.slogan: Count the image $f(A)$ of the injective map exactly.
steps.detail: The map $a \mapsto f(a)$ is a [bijection](c:bijection) from $A$ onto $f(A)$: it is onto by the definition of the image and injective by step 1. Hence $|f(A)| = |A|$.

steps.slogan: Compare the image with the target set $B$ by inclusion.
steps.detail: The image satisfies $f(A) \subseteq B$. A [subset](c:subset) of a [finite set](c:finite-set) has at most as many elements as the set, so $|f(A)| \le |B|$.

steps.slogan: Combine the two counts and contradict the hypothesis $|A| > |B|$.
steps.detail: Steps 2 and 3 give $|A| = |f(A)| \le |B|$, which contradicts $|A| > |B|$. So $f$ is not injective, and some $a \ne a'$ have $f(a) = f(a')$.

concepts.c:finite-set: Only finite sets have element counts that the proof can compare.
concepts.c:injection: The proof shows that an injection cannot exist when $|A| > |B|$.
concepts.c:cardinal-number: The principle compares the cardinalities of the two sets.
concepts.c:bijection: An injective map is a bijection onto its image, so the image has $|A|$ elements.
concepts.c:subset: The image is a subset of $B$, so it has at most $|B|$ elements.

source.note: mathlib argues by contraposition: if $t \cap u = \emptyset$, then $|t| + |u| = |t \cup u| \le |s|$ (card_union_add_card_inter, card_le_card). The proof runs the same count on the image of the map.

statement:
Let $\mu$ and $
u$ be [σ-finite measures](c:sigma-finite-measure) on a measurable space $X$, with $\mu$ [absolutely continuous](c:absolutely-continuous-measure) with respect to $
u$. Then there is a [measurable function](c:measurable-function) $f \ge 0$, the [Radon–Nikodym derivative](c:radon-nikodym-derivative) $d\mu/d
u$, with $\mu(E) = \int_E f\,d
u$ for every measurable set $E$.

hypotheses.text: The measure $\mu$ is [absolutely continuous](c:absolutely-continuous-measure) with respect to $\nu$: $\nu(E) = 0$ implies $\mu(E) = 0$.

conclusion: Some measurable $f \ge 0$ has $\mu(E) = \int_E f\,d\nu$ for every measurable set $E$.

formal.difference:
The declaration is an equivalence, $\mu \ll 
u$ if and only if $
u$ with density $d\mu/d
u$ equals $\mu$, under the class HaveLebesgueDecomposition, which σ-finite measures satisfy. The converse direction is the easy fact that a measure with a density is absolutely continuous.

proofs.name: Lebesgue decomposition
proofs.slogan: Build the largest density below $\mu$, show that the rest of $\mu$ is singular to $\nu$, and let absolute continuity remove that rest.
proofs.scope: Steps 1 to 4 treat finite measures, and step 5 extends the result to σ-finite measures. Without σ-finiteness the theorem fails: Lebesgue measure on $[0, 1]$ is absolutely continuous with respect to counting measure but has no density.

roles.why: σ-finiteness splits $X$ into pieces of finite measure, where the maximal density exists.
Absolute continuity makes the singular remainder vanish on the $\nu$-null set that carries it.

steps.slogan: Collect the functions whose $\nu$-integrals stay below $\mu$ on every set.
steps.detail: First let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be finite. Let $\mathcal{F}$ be the set of measurable $g \ge 0$ with $\int_E g\,d\nu \le \mu(E)$ for every measurable $E$. Then $0 \in \mathcal{F}$, and $\max(g, h) \in \mathcal{F}$ for $g, h \in \mathcal{F}$: split $E$ into the parts where $g \ge h$ and $g < h$.

steps.slogan: Take an increasing sequence in the class whose integrals reach the supremum.
steps.detail:
Let $s = \sup_{g \in \mathcal{F}} \int g\,d
u \le \mu(X) < \infty$. Choose $g_n \in \mathcal{F}$ with $\int g_n\,d
u 	o s$ and replace $g_n$ by $\max(g_1, \dots, g_n)$. The monotone convergence theorem gives $f = \lim g_n \in \mathcal{F}$ with $\int f\,d
u = s$.

steps.slogan: Show that the remainder $\lambda = \mu - f\nu$ is singular to $\nu$.
steps.detail:
The measure $\lambda(E) = \mu(E) - \int_E f\,d
u$ is nonnegative. If it were not singular to $
u$, a [Hahn decomposition](c:is-hahn-decomposition) of the [signed measure](c:signed-measure) $\lambda - \varepsilon
u$ would give $\varepsilon > 0$ and a set $P$ with $
u(P) > 0$ and $\lambda \ge \varepsilon
u$ on subsets of $P$. Then $f + \varepsilon\mathbf{1}_P \in \mathcal{F}$ has integral above $s$, a contradiction.

steps.slogan: Remove the singular remainder with the absolute continuity of $\mu$.
steps.detail: Singularity gives a set $N$ with $\nu(N) = 0$ and $\lambda(X \setminus N) = 0$. Absolute continuity gives $\mu(N) = 0$, so $\lambda(N) \le \mu(N) = 0$. Hence $\lambda = 0$ and $\mu(E) = \int_E f\,d\nu$.

steps.slogan: Glue the densities of the finite pieces of a countable partition.
steps.detail:
For σ-finite $\mu$ and $
u$, partition $X$ into measurable sets $A_n$ with $\mu(A_n) < \infty$ and $
u(A_n) < \infty$. Steps 1 to 4 give densities $f_n$ on the pieces $A_n$, and $f = \sum_n f_n \mathbf{1}_{A_n}$ satisfies $\mu(E) = \sum_n \mu(E \cap A_n) = \int_E f\,d
u$ by countable additivity.

concepts.c:absolutely-continuous-measure: Absolute continuity is the condition that removes the singular part.
concepts.c:measurable-function: The density must be measurable so that its integrals are defined.
concepts.c:radon-nikodym-derivative: The constructed density is the Radon–Nikodym derivative $d\mu/d\nu$.
concepts.c:is-hahn-decomposition: A Hahn decomposition finds the set where the remainder beats $\varepsilon\nu$.
concepts.c:signed-measure: The difference $\lambda - \varepsilon\nu$ is a signed measure, not a measure.

proofs.name: Hilbert space (von Neumann)
proofs.slogan: Represent integration against $\mu$ as an inner product in $L^2(\mu + \nu)$ and solve the resulting identity for the density.
proofs.scope: Steps 1 to 4 treat finite measures, and step 5 extends the result to σ-finite measures by a countable partition.

roles.why: Finite pieces make $\rho = \mu + \nu$ finite, so the functional is bounded on $L^2(\rho)$.
Absolute continuity turns $\nu(\{h = 1\}) = 0$ into $\mu(\{h = 1\}) = 0$.

steps.slogan: Define the bounded functional $\Phi(g) = \int g\,d\mu$ on $L^2(\rho)$, where $\rho = \mu + \nu$.
steps.detail: For finite $\mu$ and $\nu$ the measure $\rho$ is finite. The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives $|\Phi(g)| \le \int |g|\,d\rho \le \rho(X)^{1/2}\|g\|_{L^2(\rho)}$, so $\Phi$ is a bounded linear functional on the [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) $L^2(\rho)$.

steps.slogan: Represent the functional by a function $h$ with the Riesz representation theorem.
steps.detail: The Riesz representation theorem gives $h \in L^2(\rho)$ with $\int g\,d\mu = \int g h\,d\rho$ for all $g \in L^2(\rho)$. Since $\rho = \mu + \nu$, this reads $\int g(1 - h)\,d\mu = \int g h\,d\nu$.

steps.slogan: Show that $0 \le h < 1$ holds $\rho$-almost everywhere.
steps.detail: With $g = \mathbf{1}_E$, $\mu(E) = \int_E h\,d\rho$ lies in $[0, \rho(E)]$ for every $E$, so $0 \le h \le 1$ almost everywhere. On $Z = \{h = 1\}$ the identity of step 2 gives $\nu(Z) = 0$, so absolute continuity gives $\mu(Z) = 0$ and $\rho(Z) = 0$.

steps.slogan: Insert $g = \mathbf{1}_E(1 + h + \dots + h^n)$ and let $n$ tend to infinity.
steps.detail: Step 2 gives $\int_E (1 - h^{n+1})\,d\mu = \int_E (h + h^2 + \dots + h^{n+1})\,d\nu$. By step 3, $h^{n+1} \to 0$ almost everywhere, and monotone convergence gives $\mu(E) = \int_E f\,d\nu$ with $f = h/(1 - h)$.

steps.slogan: Extend the density to σ-finite measures over a countable partition.
steps.detail: Partition $X$ into sets $A_n$ of finite $\mu$-measure and $\nu$-measure, apply steps 1 to 4 on each $A_n$, and set $f = \sum_n f_n \mathbf{1}_{A_n}$. Countable additivity gives $\mu(E) = \int_E f\,d\nu$ for every measurable $E$.

concepts.c:absolutely-continuous-measure: Absolute continuity is the condition that removes the singular part.
concepts.c:measurable-function: The density must be measurable so that its integrals are defined.
concepts.c:radon-nikodym-derivative: The constructed density is the Radon–Nikodym derivative $d\mu/d\nu$.
concepts.c:hilbert-space: The Riesz representation theorem needs the Hilbert space $L^2(\rho)$.

source.note: John von Neumann's Hilbert-space proof, as in W. Rudin, Real and Complex Analysis, theorem 6.10.

statement: Let $X$ be a connected [compact Riemann surface](c:compact-riemann-surface) of [genus](c:genus-of-a-surface) $g$, let $D$ be a [divisor](c:divisor) on $X$ and $K$ a [canonical divisor](c:canonical-divisor). Then $\ell(D) - \ell(K - D) = \deg D + 1 - g$, where $\ell(D)$ is the dimension of the space of [meromorphic functions](c:meromorphic-function) $f$ with $f = 0$ or $\operatorname{div} f + D \ge 0$.

hypotheses.text: $X$ is a connected [compact Riemann surface](c:compact-riemann-surface) of genus $g$.
$D$ is a [divisor](c:divisor) on $X$, a finite integer combination of points.
$K$ is a [canonical divisor](c:canonical-divisor), the divisor of a nonzero meromorphic 1-form.

proofs.name: Euler characteristic and Serre duality
proofs.slogan: Show that $\chi(\mathcal{O}_D) = \deg D + 1 - g$ by adding points one at a time, then rewrite $h^1(\mathcal{O}_D)$ with Serre duality.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, with $g = \dim H^1(X, \mathcal{O})$, which equals the topological genus by Hodge theory. The finite dimension of $H^1(X, \mathcal{O})$ and Serre duality are cited theorems, not proved here.

roles.why: Compactness and connectedness give $H^0(X, \mathcal{O}) = \mathbb{C}$ and a finite $H^1(X, \mathcal{O})$ of dimension $g$, and they allow Serre duality.
The divisor is reached from $0$ by adding and removing finitely many points.
The canonical divisor identifies the sheaf of 1-forms with divisor at least $D$ with $\mathcal{O}_{K - D}$.

steps.slogan: Compute the Euler characteristic $\chi(\mathcal{O}) = 1 - g$ of the structure sheaf.
steps.detail: A holomorphic function on the compact connected surface $X$ attains its maximum modulus, so it is constant and $H^0(X, \mathcal{O}) = \mathbb{C}$. The [sheaf cohomology](c:sheaf-cohomology) group $H^1(X, \mathcal{O})$ is finite dimensional of dimension $g$. Hence $\chi(\mathcal{O}) = h^0 - h^1 = 1 - g$.

steps.slogan: Relate $\mathcal{O}_D$ and $\mathcal{O}_{D+P}$ by a [short exact sequence](c:exact-sequence) of sheaves.
steps.detail: The Laurent coefficient of order $-D(P) - 1$ at a point $P$ gives an exact sequence $0 \to \mathcal{O}_D \to \mathcal{O}_{D+P} \to \mathbb{C}_P \to 0$, where $\mathbb{C}_P$ is the [skyscraper sheaf](c:skyscraper-sheaf) at $P$. Its cohomology is $H^0 = \mathbb{C}$ and $H^1 = 0$.

steps.slogan: Read off $\chi(\mathcal{O}_{D+P}) = \chi(\mathcal{O}_D) + 1$ from the long exact sequence.
steps.detail: The sequence $0 \to H^0(\mathcal{O}_D) \to H^0(\mathcal{O}_{D+P}) \to \mathbb{C} \to H^1(\mathcal{O}_D) \to H^1(\mathcal{O}_{D+P}) \to 0$ is exact, so one sheaf has finite cohomology exactly when the other has. The alternating sum of the dimensions is zero, so $\chi(\mathcal{O}_{D+P}) = \chi(\mathcal{O}_D) + 1$.

steps.slogan: Reach every divisor from $0$ by adding and removing points one at a time.
steps.detail: Write $D = P_1 + \dots + P_r - Q_1 - \dots - Q_s$. Step 3, used forward and backward, starts from $\chi(\mathcal{O}) = 1 - g$ and gives $\chi(\mathcal{O}_D) = \deg D + 1 - g$ for every [divisor](c:divisor) $D$.

steps.slogan: Replace $h^1(\mathcal{O}_D)$ by $\ell(K - D)$ with Serre duality.
steps.detail: Serre duality gives $H^1(X, \mathcal{O}_D) \cong H^0(X, \Omega_{-D})^*$, where $\Omega_{-D}$ is the sheaf of 1-forms $\omega$ with $\omega = 0$ or $\operatorname{div}\omega \ge D$. If $K = \operatorname{div}\omega_0$, then $f \mapsto f\omega_0$ identifies $\mathcal{O}_{K - D}$ with $\Omega_{-D}$, so $h^1(\mathcal{O}_D) = \ell(K - D)$.

steps.slogan: Substitute $h^0(\mathcal{O}_D) = \ell(D)$ and $h^1(\mathcal{O}_D) = \ell(K - D)$ into the Euler characteristic.
steps.detail: By definition $H^0(X, \mathcal{O}_D)$ is the space of [meromorphic functions](c:meromorphic-function) with $f = 0$ or $\operatorname{div} f + D \ge 0$, so $h^0 = \ell(D)$. Steps 4 and 5 give $\ell(D) - \ell(K - D) = \chi(\mathcal{O}_D) = \deg D + 1 - g$.

concepts.c:compact-riemann-surface: Compactness makes the cohomology finite and holomorphic functions constant.
concepts.c:genus-of-a-surface: The genus enters as $\dim H^1(X, \mathcal{O})$ in the base case.
concepts.c:divisor: The divisor prescribes the allowed poles and the required zeros.
concepts.c:canonical-divisor: The canonical divisor turns 1-forms into functions in Serre duality.
concepts.c:meromorphic-function: The spaces $\ell(D)$ count meromorphic functions with bounded poles.
concepts.c:sheaf-cohomology: The theorem is an identity between dimensions of sheaf cohomology groups.
concepts.c:exact-sequence: The exact sequences relate the cohomology of $\mathcal{O}_D$ and $\mathcal{O}_{D+P}$.
concepts.c:skyscraper-sheaf: Adding one point changes the sheaf by a skyscraper sheaf.

source.note: The sheaf-cohomology proof of O. Forster, Lectures on Riemann Surfaces (Springer, Graduate Texts in Mathematics 81), sections 14 to 17: finiteness, the Euler characteristic count and Serre duality.

statement: Every finite [abelian group](c:abelian-group) $G$ is isomorphic to a [direct product](c:direct-product) $\mathbb{Z}/p_1^{e_1} \times \dots \times \mathbb{Z}/p_k^{e_k}$ of [cyclic groups](c:cyclic-group) of [prime power](c:prime-power) order. The list of orders $p_1^{e_1}, \dots, p_k^{e_k}$ is unique up to order.
conclusion: $G \cong \mathbb{Z}/p_1^{e_1} \times \dots \times \mathbb{Z}/p_k^{e_k}$ for primes $p_i$ and exponents $e_i \ge 1$, and the multiset of the factors $p_i^{e_i}$ depends only on $G$.

formal.difference: The declaration gives an isomorphism with a finite product of groups $\mathbb{Z}/n_i$ with $n_i > 1$, without stating that the $n_i$ are prime powers. It does not state uniqueness.

proofs.name: Primary parts and maximal-order splitting
proofs.slogan: Split $G$ into $p$-primary parts, split each part into cyclic groups by elements of maximal order, and count the quotients $p^jG/p^{j+1}G$ for uniqueness.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem; the trivial group is the empty product with $k = 0$. Steps 1 to 4 prove existence and step 5 proves uniqueness.

roles.why: Commutativity makes $G$ a $\mathbb{Z}$-module, so sums of subgroups are subgroups and multiplication by $p$ is a homomorphism.
Finiteness gives an order $|G|$ that kills every element, and it makes the induction on $|P|$ terminate.

steps.slogan: Write $G$ additively as a finite torsion module over the integers.
steps.detail: Commutativity makes $n \cdot g$ a $\mathbb{Z}$-[module](c:module) structure on $G$. Lagrange's theorem gives $|G| \cdot g = 0$ for every $g$, so $G$ is a finitely generated torsion module.

steps.slogan: Split $G$ into the direct sum of its $p$-primary components.
steps.detail: Let $|G| = \prod_p p^{a_p}$ and $G_p = \{g : p^{a_p} g = 0\}$. Bézout's identity gives integers $c_p$ with $\sum_p c_p |G|/p^{a_p} = 1$, so $g = \sum_p c_p (|G|/p^{a_p}) g$ with each term in $G_p$. Coprime orders make the sum direct: $G = \bigoplus_p G_p$.

steps.slogan: Split off the cyclic subgroup of an element of maximal order in a $p$-group.
steps.detail: Let $P$ be a finite abelian [p-group](c:p-group) and $a$ an element of maximal order $p^k$. By induction on $|P|$, $P/\langle a\rangle$ is a sum of cyclic groups, and each generator of order $p^j$ lifts to an element of order $p^j$ because $p^kP = 0$. The lifts span a complement, so $P$ is a direct sum of cyclic groups.

steps.slogan: Assemble the cyclic summands of all primary components into one product.
steps.detail: Steps 2 and 3 give $G \cong \bigoplus_p \bigoplus_i \mathbb{Z}/p^{e_{p,i}}$ with $e_{p,i} \ge 1$. In multiplicative notation this finite direct sum is the [direct product](c:direct-product) of the [cyclic groups](c:cyclic-group) $\mathbb{Z}/p_i^{e_i}$.

steps.slogan: Recover the exponents from the orders of the quotients $p^jG/p^{j+1}G$.
steps.detail: For a decomposition as in step 4, multiplication by $p$ is bijective on the factors of order prime to $p$, so $|p^jG/p^{j+1}G| = p^{m_j}$, where $m_j$ is the number of factors $\mathbb{Z}/p^e$ with $e > j$. These orders depend only on $G$, so they fix how many factors $\mathbb{Z}/p^e$ occur for each $e$.

concepts.c:abelian-group: Commutativity makes the group a module over the integers.
concepts.c:finite-group: A finite group has an order that kills all its elements.
concepts.c:direct-product: The classification writes the group as a direct product of factors.
concepts.c:cyclic-group: The factors of the decomposition are cyclic groups.
concepts.c:prime-power: Each factor has prime power order, which makes the list unique.
concepts.c:module: The integer module structure is the frame of the mathlib route.
concepts.c:p-group: The splitting step works inside one primary component, a $p$-group.

proofs.slogan: Split $G$ into $p$-primary parts, split each part into cyclic groups by elements of maximal order, and count the quotients $p^jG/p^{j+1}G$ for uniqueness.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem; the trivial group is the empty sum with $k = 0$. Steps 1 to 4 prove existence and step 5 proves uniqueness.

roles.why: Commutativity makes $G$ a $\mathbb{Z}$-module, so sums of subgroups are subgroups and multiplication by $p$ is a homomorphism.
Finiteness gives an order $|G|$ that kills every element, and it makes the induction on $|P|$ terminate.

steps.slogan: View $G$ as a finitely generated torsion module over the integers.
steps.detail: The integer multiples $n \cdot g$ make the abelian group $G$ a $\mathbb{Z}$-[module](c:module). Lagrange's theorem gives $|G| \cdot g = 0$ for every $g$, so $G$ is a finitely generated torsion module with no free part.

steps.slogan: Split $G$ into the direct sum of its $p$-primary components.
steps.detail: Let $|G| = \prod_p p^{a_p}$ and $G_p = \{g : p^{a_p} g = 0\}$. Bézout's identity gives integers $c_p$ with $\sum_p c_p |G|/p^{a_p} = 1$, so every $g$ is a sum of elements of the $G_p$. Coprime orders make the sum direct: $G = \bigoplus_p G_p$.

steps.slogan: Split off the cyclic subgroup of an element of maximal order in a $p$-group.
steps.detail: Let $P$ be a finite abelian [p-group](c:p-group) and $a$ an element of maximal order $p^k$. By induction on $|P|$, $P/\langle a\rangle$ is a sum of cyclic groups, and each generator of order $p^j$ lifts to an element of order $p^j$ because $p^kP = 0$. The lifts span a complement, so $P$ is a direct sum of cyclic groups.

steps.slogan: Collect the cyclic summands of all primary components into one direct sum.
steps.detail: Steps 2 and 3 give $G \cong \bigoplus_p \bigoplus_i \mathbb{Z}/p^{e_{p,i}}$, a finite [direct sum](c:direct-sum) of [cyclic groups](c:cyclic-group). Summands with $e_{p,i} = 0$ are trivial and are dropped, so every exponent is at least $1$.

steps.slogan: Recover the exponents from the orders of the quotients $p^jG/p^{j+1}G$.
steps.detail: For a decomposition as in step 4, multiplication by $p$ is bijective on the factors of order prime to $p$, so $|p^jG/p^{j+1}G| = p^{m_j}$, where $m_j$ is the number of factors $\mathbb{Z}/p^e$ with $e > j$. These orders depend only on $G$, so they fix how many factors $\mathbb{Z}/p^e$ occur for each $e$.

proofs.name: Relation matrix and Smith normal form
proofs.slogan: Present $G$ by an integer relation matrix, diagonalize the matrix by row and column operations, and split the diagonal factors by the Chinese remainder theorem.
proofs.scope: Existence in steps 1 to 4 and uniqueness in step 5; the trivial group gives the empty sum.

roles.why: Commutativity makes $G$ a quotient of the free abelian group $\mathbb{Z}^n$.
Finiteness gives finitely many generators and a relation subgroup of full rank $n$.

steps.slogan: Present $G$ as the quotient of $\mathbb{Z}^n$ by a relation subgroup $K$.
steps.detail: Choose generators $g_1, \dots, g_n$ of $G$, and map the basis vector $e_i$ to $g_i$; commutativity makes this a surjective homomorphism $\mathbb{Z}^n \to G$ with kernel $K$. Since $|G|\,\mathbb{Z}^n \subseteq K$, the subgroup $K$ is free of rank $n$, the image $A\mathbb{Z}^n$ of an integer matrix $A$ with $\det A \ne 0$.

steps.slogan: Diagonalize $A$ by invertible integer row and column operations.
steps.detail: Euclidean steps on rows and columns bring $A$ to its [Smith normal form](c:smith-normal-form) $UAV = \operatorname{diag}(d_1, \dots, d_n)$, with $U$ and $V$ invertible over $\mathbb{Z}$ and $d_1 \mid d_2 \mid \dots \mid d_n$. All $d_i$ are positive because $\det A \neq 0$.

steps.slogan: Read off $G \cong \bigoplus_i \mathbb{Z}/d_i$ from the diagonal form.
steps.detail: Let $D = \operatorname{diag}(d_1, \dots, d_n)$. Then $K = A\mathbb{Z}^n = U^{-1}D\mathbb{Z}^n$, so in the basis of $\mathbb{Z}^n$ given by the columns of $U^{-1}$ the subgroup $K$ is $d_1\mathbb{Z} \oplus \dots \oplus d_n\mathbb{Z}$. Hence $G \cong \mathbb{Z}^n/K \cong \bigoplus_i \mathbb{Z}/d_i$.

steps.slogan: Split each factor $\mathbb{Z}/d_i$ into prime power factors by the Chinese remainder theorem.
steps.detail: If $d = \prod_p p^{a_p}$, the Chinese remainder theorem gives $\mathbb{Z}/d \cong \bigoplus_p \mathbb{Z}/p^{a_p}$, because distinct prime powers are coprime. Dropping the trivial factors gives a [direct sum](c:direct-sum) of [cyclic groups](c:cyclic-group) of [prime power](c:prime-power) order.

steps.slogan: Recover the exponents from the orders of the quotients $p^jG/p^{j+1}G$.
steps.detail: For a decomposition as in step 4, multiplication by $p$ is bijective on the factors of order prime to $p$, so $|p^jG/p^{j+1}G| = p^{m_j}$, where $m_j$ is the number of factors $\mathbb{Z}/p^e$ with $e > j$. These orders depend only on $G$, so they fix how many factors $\mathbb{Z}/p^e$ occur for each $e$.

statement: Let $C$ be a [locally small](c:locally-small) [category](c:category), $c$ an object of $C$ and $X\colon C^{\mathrm{op}} \to \mathbf{Set}$ a [presheaf](c:presheaf). Then $\alpha \mapsto \alpha_c(\mathrm{id}_c)$ is a bijection from the set of [natural transformations](c:natural-transformation) $C(-, c) \Rightarrow X$ to the set $X(c)$, and this bijection is natural in $c$ and in $X$.

hypotheses.text: The category $C$ is [locally small](c:locally-small): each [hom-set](c:hom-set) $C(d, c)$ is a set.
$X$ is a [presheaf](c:presheaf) of sets on $C$, a [functor](c:functor) $C^{\mathrm{op}} \to \mathbf{Set}$.

conclusion: $\operatorname{Nat}(C(-, c), X) \cong X(c)$ by $\alpha \mapsto \alpha_c(\mathrm{id}_c)$, naturally in $c$ and $X$.

proofs.name: Evaluation at the identity
proofs.slogan: Evaluate a natural transformation at $\mathrm{id}_c$, and rebuild the transformation from that one value by naturality.
proofs.scope: The whole lemma, including naturality. Local smallness makes $C(-, c)$ a presheaf of sets, the [representable functor](c:representable-functor) of $c$.

roles.why: Local smallness makes $C(-, c)$ a presheaf of sets, so natural transformations into $X$ are defined.
Functoriality of $X$ gives $X(f \circ h) = X(h) \circ X(f)$, which makes the rebuilt family natural.

steps.slogan: Define $\Phi(\alpha) = \alpha_c(\mathrm{id}_c)$ for each [natural transformation](c:natural-transformation) $\alpha\colon C(-, c) \Rightarrow X$.
steps.detail: Because $C$ is locally small, $C(-, c)$ is a presheaf of sets, and $\alpha$ has a component $\alpha_c\colon C(c, c) \to X(c)$. Its value at $\mathrm{id}_c$ is an element $\Phi(\alpha) \in X(c)$.

steps.slogan: Show that naturality fixes every component of $\alpha$ by its value at $\mathrm{id}_c$.
steps.detail: For $f\colon d \to c$, write $f = \mathrm{id}_c \circ f = C(f, c)(\mathrm{id}_c)$. Naturality of $\alpha$ along $f$ gives $\alpha_d(f) = X(f)(\alpha_c(\mathrm{id}_c))$. Hence two transformations with the same value of $\Phi$ are equal, and $\Phi$ is injective.

steps.slogan: Build a natural transformation $\alpha^x$ from each element $x \in X(c)$.
steps.detail: Set $\alpha^x_d(f) = X(f)(x)$ for $f\colon d \to c$. For $h\colon e \to d$, functoriality of the [presheaf](c:presheaf) gives $\alpha^x_e(f \circ h) = X(h)(X(f)(x)) = X(h)(\alpha^x_d(f))$, so $\alpha^x$ is natural.

steps.slogan: Check that $x \mapsto \alpha^x$ is inverse to $\Phi$.
steps.detail: First, $\Phi(\alpha^x) = X(\mathrm{id}_c)(x) = x$. Step 2 gives $\alpha = \alpha^{\Phi(\alpha)}$ for every $\alpha$. So $\Phi$ is a bijection with inverse $x \mapsto \alpha^x$.

steps.slogan: Check that $\Phi$ commutes with maps of presheaves and with maps $g\colon c' \to c$.
steps.detail: For $\theta\colon X \Rightarrow X'$, $\Phi(\theta \circ \alpha) = \theta_c(\alpha_c(\mathrm{id}_c)) = \theta_c(\Phi(\alpha))$. For $g\colon c' \to c$, step 2 gives $\Phi(\alpha \circ C(-, g)) = \alpha_{c'}(g) = X(g)(\Phi(\alpha))$. So the bijection is a [natural isomorphism](c:natural-isomorphism).

concepts.c:locally-small: Local smallness makes the hom-functor $C(-, c)$ take values in sets.
concepts.c:category: The lemma holds in every locally small category.
concepts.c:presheaf: The target $X$ is a presheaf whose functoriality drives the construction.
concepts.c:natural-transformation: The lemma counts the natural transformations out of $C(-, c)$.
concepts.c:hom-set: The representable presheaf sends $d$ to the hom-set $C(d, c)$.
concepts.c:functor: A presheaf is a contravariant functor into sets.
concepts.c:representable-functor: The source $C(-, c)$ is the representable functor of $c$.
concepts.c:natural-isomorphism: Naturality in $c$ and $X$ makes the bijection a natural isomorphism.

statement: Let $f$ be [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) on an [open set](c:open-set) $U \subseteq \mathbb{C}$. If the closed [disk](c:ball) $|z - z_0| \le r$ lies in $U$, then $f(z) = \sum_{n \ge 0} a_n (z - z_0)^n$ for $|z - z_0| < r$, a convergent [power series](c:power-series). Hence $f$ is [analytic](c:analytic-function) on $U$.

hypotheses.text: $f$ is [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) on $U$: it has a complex derivative at every point of $U$.
The closed disk $|z - z_0| \le r$ with $r > 0$ lies in $U$.

conclusion: For $|z - z_0| < r$, $f(z) = \sum_{n \ge 0} a_n (z - z_0)^n$ with $a_n = \frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_{|w - z_0| = r} \frac{f(w)}{(w - z_0)^{n+1}}\,dw$, and $f$ is analytic on $U$.

formal.difference: The declaration allows values in a complex Banach space and asks that $f$ be complex differentiable on a neighborhood of $z_0$. It gives analyticity at $z_0$ without the radius $r$ or the coefficient formula.

proofs.name: Cauchy formula and geometric series
proofs.slogan: Write $f$ by the Cauchy integral formula on a circle, expand the kernel as a geometric series, and integrate term by term.
proofs.scope: The expansion on each closed disk in $U$; analyticity at every point follows because the open set $U$ contains such a disk around each of its points.

roles.why: Openness gives a disk inside $U$ around every point, so the expansion holds near every point of $U$.
Holomorphy near the closed disk gives the Cauchy integral formula and a continuous, bounded $f$ on the circle.
The closed disk in $U$ supplies the circle of integration and the ratio $|z - z_0|/r < 1$.

steps.slogan: Write $f(z)$ by the Cauchy integral formula on the circle $|w - z_0| = r$.
steps.detail: The compact closed disk has a slightly larger open disk inside $U$, where $f$ is [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function). The Cauchy integral formula gives the [contour integral](c:contour-integral) $f(z) = \frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_{|w - z_0| = r} \frac{f(w)}{w - z}\,dw$ for $|z - z_0| < r$.

steps.slogan: Expand the Cauchy kernel $1/(w - z)$ as a [geometric series](c:geometric-series) in $(z - z_0)/(w - z_0)$.
steps.detail: For $|w - z_0| = r$ and $q = |z - z_0|/r < 1$, $\frac{1}{w - z} = \frac{1}{w - z_0} \cdot \frac{1}{1 - (z - z_0)/(w - z_0)} = \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{(z - z_0)^n}{(w - z_0)^{n+1}}$. The $n$-th term has modulus $q^n/r$.

steps.slogan: Integrate the series term by term, using its [uniform convergence](c:uniform-convergence) on the circle.
steps.detail: The continuous $f$ is bounded by some $M$ on the circle, so the $n$-th term of $f(w)/(w - z)$ is at most $Mq^n/r$ for every $w$. Uniform convergence allows the exchange of sum and integral, so $f(z) = \sum_n a_n (z - z_0)^n$ with $a_n$ as in the conclusion.

steps.slogan: Find such a disk around every point of $U$ to conclude analyticity.
steps.detail: For $z_0 \in U$, openness gives $r > 0$ with the closed disk $|z - z_0| \le r$ inside $U$. Steps 1 to 3 give a [power series](c:power-series) for $f$ that converges on $|z - z_0| < r$, so $f$ is [analytic](c:analytic-function) at $z_0$.

concepts.c:open-set: An open set contains a disk around each of its points.
concepts.c:ball: The closed disk supplies the circle of integration.
concepts.c:power-series: The conclusion is a power series expansion around $z_0$.

concepts.c:geometric-series: The Cauchy kernel expands as a geometric series in $z - z_0$.

statement: For every $n \ge 0$ and every [continuous](c:continuous-function) map $f\colon S^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$, some point $x$ of the [sphere](c:sphere) $S^n$ has $f(x) = f(-x)$; that is, $f$ takes the same value at two points exchanged by the [antipodal map](c:antipodal-map).

proofs.name: Odd maps and degree
proofs.slogan: Turn a counterexample into an odd map $S^n \to S^{n-1}$, whose restriction to the equator has odd degree but also degree zero.
proofs.scope: For $n = 0$ the claim holds because $\mathbb{R}^0$ is a point, and for $n = 1$ the proof ends in step 3 by connectedness. Step 4 rests on Borsuk's theorem that an odd self-map of a sphere has odd degree, proved with homology mod $2$.

roles.why: Continuity of $f$ makes the normalized difference $g$ continuous, so its restriction has a degree and extends over the hemisphere.

steps.slogan: Assume that $f(x) \neq f(-x)$ for every point $x$ of $S^n$.
steps.detail: The proof is by contradiction, for $n \ge 1$. Under this assumption the difference $f(x) - f(-x)$ never vanishes on the [sphere](c:sphere).

steps.slogan: Normalize the difference to a continuous odd map $g\colon S^n \to S^{n-1}$.
steps.detail: Set $g(x) = (f(x) - f(-x))/|f(x) - f(-x)|$. It is [continuous](c:continuous-function) because $f$ is continuous and the denominator never vanishes, and $g(-x) = -g(x)$, so $g$ commutes with the [antipodal map](c:antipodal-map).

steps.slogan: Restrict $g$ to the equator $S^{n-1}$ to get an odd map $h\colon S^{n-1} \to S^{n-1}$.
steps.detail: The equator is invariant under $x \mapsto -x$, so $h$ is odd. For $n = 1$ the assumption already fails: $g$ maps the connected circle $S^1$ continuously into the two points of $S^0$, so $g$ is constant, against $g(-x) = -g(x)$.

steps.slogan: Give the odd map $h$ an odd [degree](c:degree-of-a-map) when $n \ge 2$.
steps.detail: Borsuk's theorem says that an odd map $S^m \to S^m$ with $m \ge 1$ has odd degree. Its proof compares the maps on [homology](c:homology) with coefficients in $\mathbb{Z}/2$ induced by $h$ and by its quotient map of projective spaces. So $\deg h$ is odd, in particular not zero.

steps.slogan: Extend $h$ over the upper hemisphere to show that $\deg h = 0$.
steps.detail: The upper hemisphere is a closed [ball](c:ball) with boundary $S^{n-1}$, and $g$ restricted to it extends $h$. Contracting the ball to its center gives a [null-homotopy](c:null-homotopy) of $h$, and homotopic maps have equal degrees, so $\deg h = 0$.

steps.slogan: Compare the two degrees and reject the assumption.
steps.detail: Step 4 gives an odd degree and step 5 gives degree zero, which is even. So the assumption is false, and some $x \in S^n$ has $f(x) = f(-x)$.

concepts.c:continuous-function: Continuity passes from $f$ to the odd map $g$ and its restriction.
concepts.c:sphere: The theorem concerns maps defined on the sphere $S^n$.
concepts.c:antipodal-map: The map $g$ commutes with the antipodal map, which forces an odd degree.
concepts.c:degree-of-a-map: The degree of the equator map is both odd and zero.
concepts.c:homology: Degree and Borsuk's parity theorem are read on homology groups.
concepts.c:ball: The hemisphere is a ball, so the equator map extends over it.
concepts.c:null-homotopy: A null-homotopic map of spheres has degree zero.

source.note: The degree proof in A. Hatcher, Algebraic Topology (Cambridge University Press, 2002), section 2.B, where an odd map of spheres is shown to have odd degree.

statement: Let a [finite group](c:finite-group) $G$ [act](c:group-action) on a finite set $X$, and let $X^g = \{x \in X : gx = x\}$ be the set of [fixed points](c:fixed-point) of $g$. Then the number of [orbits](c:orbit) is $\frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g \in G} |X^g|$.

formal.difference: The declaration states $\sum_{g} |X^g| = |X/G| \cdot |G|$, the same identity multiplied by $|G|$. It asks only that $G$, each $X^g$ and the orbit set be finite, not $X$.

proofs.name: Double counting of fixed pairs
proofs.slogan: Count the pairs $(g, x)$ with $gx = x$ by group elements and by points, then sum the orbit-stabilizer ratios over each orbit.
proofs.scope: The whole lemma. For $X = \emptyset$ both sides are $0$.

roles.why: Finiteness of $G$ makes $|G|$ and the orbit sizes finite numbers that the proof can divide by.
The action defines the fixed sets, the [stabilizers](c:stabilizer) and the orbits that the proof counts.
Finiteness of $X$ makes the set of fixed pairs finite and gives finitely many orbits.

steps.slogan: Count the set $F = \{(g, x) : gx = x\}$ by group elements and by points.
steps.detail: Counting $F$ by its first coordinate gives $|F| = \sum_{g \in G} |X^g|$. Counting it by its second coordinate gives $|F| = \sum_{x \in X} |G_x|$, where $G_x$ is the [stabilizer](c:stabilizer) of $x$.

steps.slogan: Replace each stabilizer size by $|G|/|Gx|$ with the orbit-stabilizer bijection.
steps.detail: The map $gG_x \mapsto gx$ is a bijection from the cosets of $G_x$ onto the [orbit](c:orbit) $Gx$. Lagrange's theorem gives $|G| = |G_x|\,|Gx|$, so $|G_x| = |G|/|Gx|$.

steps.slogan: Sum $1/|Gx|$ over the points of each orbit to get one per orbit.
steps.detail: The orbits partition $X$, and every $x$ in an orbit $O$ has $|Gx| = |O|$. So $\sum_{x \in X} 1/|Gx| = \sum_{O} \sum_{x \in O} 1/|O| = |X/G|$.

steps.slogan: Combine the three counts and divide by $|G|$.
steps.detail: Steps 1 to 3 give $\sum_{g} |X^g| = \sum_{x} |G|/|Gx| = |G|\,|X/G|$. Divide by $|G| \ge 1$ to get the number of orbits.

concepts.c:finite-group: The group must be finite so that the average over $G$ makes sense.
concepts.c:group-action: The action supplies the fixed points, the stabilizers and the orbits.
concepts.c:fixed-point: The lemma averages the numbers of fixed points of the group elements.
concepts.c:orbit: The lemma counts the orbits of the action.
concepts.c:finite-set: A finite set has finitely many fixed pairs and finitely many orbits.
concepts.c:stabilizer: Stabilizer sizes link the pair count to the orbit sizes.

source.note: mathlib builds a bijection from the pairs $(g, x)$ with $gx = x$ to the product of the orbit set and $G$ (sigmaFixedByEquivOrbitsProdGroup), which uses the orbit-stabilizer bijection on each orbit, and compares cardinalities (Fintype.card_sigma, Fintype.card_prod).

statement: Let $\Sigma$ be a finite alphabet. A [language](c:language) $L \subseteq \Sigma^*$ is [regular](c:regular-language) if and only if $L$ is the set of finite [words](c:word) that satisfy some [sentence](c:sentence) of [monadic second-order logic](c:monadic-second-order-logic) with the order $<$ on positions and the letter predicates $P_a$.
conclusion: $L$ is recognized by a [finite automaton](c:finite-automaton) exactly when $L$ is definable by a monadic second-order sentence.

proofs.name: Runs as set variables, formulas as automata
proofs.slogan: Describe an accepting run by existential set variables, and build an automaton for each formula by induction on its structure.
proofs.scope: Both directions; the empty word is handled by one extra disjunct in the sentence of step 1. The successor relation $y = x + 1$ is first-order definable from $<$.

roles.why: A finite alphabet gives finitely many letter predicates and finite automata over the alphabets $\Sigma \times \{0, 1\}^k$.

steps.slogan: Encode an accepting run of a deterministic automaton by one set variable per state.
steps.detail: Let a [deterministic finite automaton](c:dfa) $A$ have states $q_1, \dots, q_m$, and let $X_j$ hold the positions after which $A$ is in state $q_j$. The sentence $\exists X_1 \dots \exists X_m$ says that the $X_j$ partition the positions, that the first and each next position follow the transition map, and that the last position lies in an accepting $X_j$.

steps.slogan: Read a formula with free set variables as a language over $\Sigma \times \{0, 1\}^k$.
steps.detail: A word with sets $X_1, \dots, X_k$ of positions is a word over $\Sigma \times \{0, 1\}^k$ whose $j$-th track marks the positions in $X_j$. First-order variables become singleton sets, so the atomic formulas reduce to $X \subseteq Y$, $X \subseteq P_a$, $\mathrm{Sing}(X)$ and $X < Y$.

steps.slogan: Build a finite automaton for each atomic formula.
steps.detail: Each atomic formula is a simple condition on the tracks. For example, $X \subseteq Y$ forbids a letter with $1$ on track $X$ and $0$ on track $Y$, and $\mathrm{Sing}(X)$ needs exactly one $1$ on track $X$; a [finite automaton](c:finite-automaton) with at most three states checks each condition.

steps.slogan: Close the recognized languages under disjunction and negation.
steps.detail: A product automaton recognizes the union of two [regular languages](c:regular-language). For negation, the subset construction gives a deterministic automaton, and the exchange of accepting and rejecting states gives the complement; an intersection with the words whose first-order tracks are singletons keeps the encoding valid.

steps.slogan: Close the recognized languages under existential quantification by erasing a track.
steps.detail: The formula $\exists X\,\varphi$ defines the image of the language of $\varphi$ under the map that deletes track $X$. A [nondeterministic automaton](c:nfa) guesses the deleted bits, so the image is regular.

steps.slogan: Combine both directions by induction on the structure of formulas.
steps.detail: Steps 3 to 5 give every formula a regular language over its extended alphabet; for a [sentence](c:sentence), $k = 0$ and the language is $L \subseteq \Sigma^*$ itself. With step 1, the regular languages are exactly the languages definable in [monadic second-order logic](c:monadic-second-order-logic).

concepts.c:language: The theorem compares two ways to describe a language of finite words.
concepts.c:regular-language: Regular languages are the automaton side of the equivalence.
concepts.c:word: Positions of a word are the elements that the formulas quantify over.
concepts.c:sentence: A sentence has no free variables, so it defines a language over $\Sigma$.
concepts.c:monadic-second-order-logic: Set quantifiers of the logic express the hidden run of an automaton.
concepts.c:finite-automaton: Each formula gets a finite automaton for its language.
concepts.c:dfa: A deterministic automaton has one run, which set variables can describe.
concepts.c:nfa: Nondeterminism lets the automaton guess the bits of an erased track.

source.note: Büchi's translation between automata and formulas, as in W. Thomas, Languages, automata, and logic, in Handbook of Formal Languages, volume 3 (Springer, 1997).

statement: Let $f = u + iv$ be defined on an open set containing $z_0 = x_0 + iy_0$ in $\mathbb{C}$. Then $f$ has a [complex derivative](c:complex-derivative) at $z_0$ if and only if $f$ is [differentiable](c:differentiable-function) at $z_0$ as a map $\mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ and its [partial derivatives](c:partial-derivative) satisfy $u_x = v_y$ and $u_y = -v_x$ at $(x_0, y_0)$.

hypotheses.text: The function $f\colon U \to \mathbb{C}$ is defined on an [open set](c:open-set) $U$ that contains $z_0$.

conclusion: $f'(z_0)$ exists exactly when $f$ is real differentiable at $z_0$ with $u_x = v_y$ and $u_y = -v_x$ there; then $f'(z_0) = u_x + iv_x$.

formal.difference: The declaration allows values in any complex normed space and writes the Cauchy-Riemann condition as $Df(z_0)(i) = i\,Df(z_0)(1)$ for the real derivative $Df(z_0)$, not in partial derivatives.

proofs.name: Complex-linear real derivative
proofs.slogan: A real-linear map of $\mathbb{C}$ is complex-linear exactly when it sends $i$ to $i$ times the image of $1$, and this condition is the pair of Cauchy-Riemann equations.
proofs.scope: Both directions of the equivalence at the single point $z_0$.

roles.why: An open set around $z_0$ lets the difference quotients and the real derivative be defined at $z_0$.

steps.slogan: Restrict the complex derivative to a real-[linear map](c:linear-map) of $\mathbb{C}$.
steps.detail: If $f'(z_0) = a$ exists, then $f(z_0 + h) = f(z_0) + ah + o(|h|)$. The map $h \mapsto ah$ is real-linear, so $f$ is real differentiable at $z_0$ with $Df(z_0)h = ah$, and $Df(z_0)(i) = i\,Df(z_0)(1)$.

steps.slogan: Show that a real-linear map $L$ with $L(i) = iL(1)$ is multiplication by $L(1)$.
steps.detail: For $h = s + ti$ with real $s$ and $t$, real linearity gives $L(h) = sL(1) + tL(i) = sL(1) + tiL(1) = hL(1)$. So $L$ is complex-linear.

steps.slogan: Turn a real derivative with $L(i) = iL(1)$ into a complex derivative.
steps.detail: If $f$ is real differentiable at $z_0$ with $L = Df(z_0)$ and $L(i) = iL(1)$, step 2 gives $f(z_0 + h) = f(z_0) + L(1)h + o(|h|)$. Divide by $h$: the difference quotient tends to $L(1)$, so $f'(z_0) = L(1)$.

steps.slogan: Write the condition $L(i) = iL(1)$ in [partial derivatives](c:partial-derivative).
steps.detail: The real derivative has $L(1) = u_x + iv_x$ and $L(i) = u_y + iv_y$, and $iL(1) = -v_x + iu_x$. Equal real parts and equal imaginary parts give $u_y = -v_x$ and $v_y = u_x$.

steps.slogan: Combine both directions with the partial-derivative form of the condition.
steps.detail: Step 1 gives the forward direction and steps 2 and 3 give the converse, both with the condition $L(i) = iL(1)$. Step 4 turns that condition into $u_x = v_y$ and $u_y = -v_x$, and step 3 gives $f'(z_0) = L(1) = u_x + iv_x$.

concepts.c:complex-derivative: The theorem characterizes when the complex derivative exists.
concepts.c:differentiable-function: Real differentiability supplies the real-linear map $Df(z_0)$.
concepts.c:partial-derivative: The Cauchy-Riemann equations are relations between partial derivatives.
concepts.c:open-set: An open domain makes the derivative at $z_0$ a two-sided limit.
concepts.c:linear-map: Complex differentiability means that the real derivative is complex-linear.

statement: Let $E, F, G$ be [normed spaces](c:normed-space) over $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. If $f\colon E \to F$ is [differentiable](c:differentiable-function) at $x$ and $g\colon F \to G$ is differentiable at $f(x)$, then the [composition](c:composition-of-functions) $g \circ f$ is differentiable at $x$ with [derivative](c:derivative) $D(g \circ f)(x) = Dg(f(x)) \circ Df(x)$. In one variable, $(g \circ f)'(x) = g'(f(x))\,f'(x)$.

hypotheses.text: $f$ is [differentiable](c:differentiable-function) at $x$, with derivative the bounded [linear map](c:linear-map) $A = Df(x)$.
$g$ is differentiable at $f(x)$, with derivative the bounded linear map $B = Dg(f(x))$.

conclusion: $g \circ f$ is differentiable at $x$ and $D(g \circ f)(x) = B \circ A$.

formal.difference: The declaration works over any nontrivially normed field and states only the formula for fderiv. The differentiability of $g \circ f$ is the separate fact HasFDerivAt.comp.

proofs.name: Composition of linear approximations
proofs.slogan: Insert the linear approximation of $f$ into that of $g$, and show that both error terms stay small compared with $|h|$.
proofs.scope: The whole rule in any normed spaces; the one-variable formula is the case $E = F = G = \mathbb{R}$, where $B \circ A$ is multiplication by $g'(f(x))\,f'(x)$.

roles.why: Differentiability of $f$ gives the expansion $f(x + h) = f(x) + Ah + r(h)$ with a small error $r(h)$.
Differentiability of $g$ at $f(x)$ gives the expansion of $g$ along the increment $k(h)$.

steps.slogan: Write the increment of $f$ as $k(h) = Ah + r(h)$ with $|r(h)| = o(|h|)$.
steps.detail: Differentiability of $f$ at $x$ gives $k(h) = f(x + h) - f(x) = Ah + r(h)$, where $|r(h)|/|h| \to 0$ as $h \to 0$.

steps.slogan: Bound the increment by $|k(h)| \le (\|A\| + 1)|h|$ for small $h$.
steps.detail: For small $|h|$, $|r(h)| \le |h|$. The [linear map](c:linear-map) $A$ is bounded, so $|k(h)| \le \|A\|\,|h| + |h|$; in particular $k(h) \to 0$.

steps.slogan: Expand $g$ at $f(x)$ along the increment $k(h)$ and control its error.
steps.detail: Differentiability of $g$ gives $g(f(x) + k) = g(f(x)) + Bk + s(k)$, where for every $\varepsilon > 0$, $|s(k)| \le \varepsilon |k|$ for small $|k|$. By step 2, $|s(k(h))| \le \varepsilon(\|A\| + 1)|h|$ for small $|h|$, so $s(k(h)) = o(|h|)$.

steps.slogan: Split the linear term $Bk(h)$ into $BAh$ and a small error.
steps.detail: Linearity gives $Bk(h) = BAh + Br(h)$, and $|Br(h)| \le \|B\|\,|r(h)| = o(|h|)$ because $B$ is bounded.

steps.slogan: Add the two error terms to get the [derivative](c:derivative) $B \circ A$.
steps.detail: Since $f(x + h) = f(x) + k(h)$, steps 3 and 4 give $g(f(x + h)) = g(f(x)) + BAh + Br(h) + s(k(h))$, and the triangle inequality makes the last two terms together $o(|h|)$. So $g \circ f$ is differentiable at $x$ with derivative the bounded linear map $B \circ A$.

concepts.c:normed-space: Norms measure the increments and the errors of the approximations.
concepts.c:differentiable-function: Differentiability gives a linear approximation with a small error.
concepts.c:composition-of-functions: The rule computes the derivative of the composition $g \circ f$.
concepts.c:derivative: The derivative of the composition is the composition of the derivatives.
concepts.c:linear-map: Bounded linear maps send small errors to small errors.

source.note: mathlib applies HasFDerivAt.comp, whose proof (HasFDerivAtFilter.comp) splits the error into the little-o error of $g$ along the increment of $f$ (isLittleOTVS.comp_tendsto, isBigOTVS_sub) plus $g'$ applied to the error of $f$; HasFDerivAt.fderiv then reads off fderiv.

statement: Let $H$ be the [joint distribution](c:joint-distribution) function of a random vector $(X_1, \dots, X_d)$ with [marginal distribution](c:marginal-distribution) functions $F_1, \dots, F_d$. Then there is a [copula](c:copula) $C$ with $H(x_1, \dots, x_d) = C(F_1(x_1), \dots, F_d(x_d))$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$. If every $F_i$ is continuous, then $C$ is unique.

hypotheses.text: $H$ is the [joint distribution](c:joint-distribution) function of a random vector in $\mathbb{R}^d$, with [marginal distribution](c:marginal-distribution) functions $F_1, \dots, F_d$.
For the uniqueness part, every marginal [distribution function](c:distribution-function) $F_i$ is continuous.

conclusion: Some copula $C$ has $H(x) = C(F_1(x_1), \dots, F_d(x_d))$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$, and $C$ is unique when every $F_i$ is continuous.

proofs.name: Distributional transform
proofs.slogan: Randomize the jumps of each marginal to get uniform variables that recover the original ones, and take their joint distribution function as the copula.
proofs.scope: Existence for arbitrary marginals in steps 1 to 5, and uniqueness for continuous marginals in step 6. Without continuity, $C$ is unique only on the product of the ranges of the $F_i$.

roles.why: The random vector with distribution $H$ supplies the coordinates $X_i$ that the transform makes uniform.
Continuous marginals have ranges that contain $(0, 1)$, where the formula fixes $C$.

steps.slogan: Take a random vector $X$ with distribution $H$ and an independent uniform variable $V$.
steps.detail: On a product probability space, let $X = (X_1, \dots, X_d)$ have joint distribution function $H$, and let $V$ have the [uniform distribution](c:uniform-distribution) on $[0, 1]$ and be independent of $X$.

steps.slogan: Define $U_i = F_i(X_i-) + V\,(F_i(X_i) - F_i(X_i-))$ and show that $U_i$ is uniform.
steps.detail: For $u \in (0, 1)$, let $t = \inf\{s : F_i(s) \ge u\}$. Then $U_i \le u$ holds when $X_i < t$, fails almost surely when $X_i > t$, and holds with conditional probability $(u - F_i(t-))/(F_i(t) - F_i(t-))$ when $X_i = t$. So $P(U_i \le u) = F_i(t-) + (u - F_i(t-)) = u$.

steps.slogan: Recover each coordinate as $X_i = F_i^{-1}(U_i)$ almost surely.
steps.detail: Here $F_i^{-1}(u) = \inf\{s : F_i(s) \ge u\}$. Since $F_i(X_i-) \le U_i \le F_i(X_i)$, the value $F_i^{-1}(U_i)$ is at most $X_i$, and it is smaller only if $U_i = F_i(X_i-)$ and $F_i$ is constant on an interval left of $X_i$, an event of probability zero.

steps.slogan: Take the joint distribution function $C$ of $(U_1, \dots, U_d)$ as the copula.
steps.detail: By step 2 every $U_i$ is uniform on $[0, 1]$, so the [distribution function](c:distribution-function) $C(u) = P(U_1 \le u_1, \dots, U_d \le u_d)$ has uniform marginals. So $C$ is a [copula](c:copula).

steps.slogan: Rewrite $H$ through $C$ with the rule $F_i^{-1}(u) \le x \iff u \le F_i(x)$.
steps.detail: The rule holds because $F_i$ is nondecreasing and right-continuous. With step 3, $H(x) = P(F_i^{-1}(U_i) \le x_i \text{ for all } i) = P(U_i \le F_i(x_i) \text{ for all } i) = C(F_1(x_1), \dots, F_d(x_d))$.

steps.slogan: Show that the formula fixes $C$ on $[0, 1]^d$ when the marginals are continuous.
steps.detail: Any copula $C'$ with the same formula agrees with $C$ on the product of the ranges of the $F_i$. For continuous $F_i$ each range contains $(0, 1)$, and a copula is continuous because $|C(u) - C(v)| \le \sum_i |u_i - v_i|$, so $C' = C$.

concepts.c:joint-distribution: The theorem factors the joint distribution function through the marginals.
concepts.c:marginal-distribution: The marginals are the inputs that the copula combines.
concepts.c:copula: The copula carries all the dependence between the coordinates.
concepts.c:distribution-function: Distribution functions and their generalized inverses drive every step.
concepts.c:uniform-distribution: The transformed variables are uniform, so their joint law is a copula.

source.note: The distributional-transform proof of L. Rüschendorf, On the distributional transform, Sklar's theorem, and the empirical copula process, Journal of Statistical Planning and Inference (2009).

new_concepts.name: copula
new_concepts.reminder: A copula is a joint distribution function on the unit cube whose marginals are uniform.
new_concepts.definition: A $d$-dimensional copula is the [distribution function](c:distribution-function) $C(u) = P(U_1 \le u_1, \dots, U_d \le u_d)$ of a random vector $(U_1, \dots, U_d)$ whose coordinates each have the [uniform distribution](c:uniform-distribution) on $[0, 1]$.

statement: For every real number $x$ and every integer $n$, $(\cos x + i\sin x)^n = \cos nx + i\sin nx$, where $i$ is the [imaginary unit](c:imaginary-unit) of the [complex numbers](c:complex-number) and $\cos$ and $\sin$ are the [trigonometric functions](c:trigonometric-function).

hypotheses.text: The angle $x$ is a real number.

conclusion: $(\cos x + i\sin x)^n = \cos nx + i\sin nx$.

formal.difference: The declaration takes $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and a complex $z$, so it allows complex angles but omits negative exponents.

proofs.name: Euler's formula
proofs.slogan: Write $\cos x + i\sin x$ as $e^{ix}$, raise the exponential to the $n$-th power, and convert back.
proofs.scope: All integers $n$; step 3 treats $n < 0$ with $e^{-a} = 1/e^{a}$. For $n = 0$ both sides equal $1$.

roles.why: Euler's formula applies to the angle $x$ and to its multiples $nx$.
An integer exponent is a repeated product or the inverse of one, which matches the exponent rule.

steps.slogan: Write $\cos x + i\sin x = e^{ix}$ by Euler's formula.
steps.detail: Euler's formula $e^{i\theta} = \cos\theta + i\sin\theta$ follows from the power series of the [exponential function](c:exponential-function), cosine and sine. With $\theta = x$ it gives $\cos x + i\sin x = e^{ix}$.

steps.slogan: Raise $e^{ix}$ to a natural power with the rule $e^{a+b} = e^a e^b$.
steps.detail: Induction on $n \ge 0$ gives $(e^{ix})^n = e^{inx}$: the case $n = 0$ is $1 = e^0$, and $(e^{ix})^{n+1} = e^{inx}e^{ix} = e^{i(n+1)x}$.

steps.slogan: Extend the power rule to negative exponents with $e^{-a} = 1/e^{a}$.
steps.detail: For $n = -m$ with $m > 0$, the identity $e^{a}e^{-a} = e^{0} = 1$ and step 2 give $(e^{ix})^{-m} = 1/e^{imx} = e^{-imx} = e^{inx}$.

steps.slogan: Convert $e^{inx}$ back to $\cos nx + i\sin nx$ by Euler's formula.
steps.detail: Euler's formula with the angle $nx$ gives $e^{inx} = \cos nx + i\sin nx$. Steps 1 to 3 give $(\cos x + i\sin x)^n = (e^{ix})^n = e^{inx}$ for every integer $n$, so the formula follows.

concepts.c:imaginary-unit: The imaginary unit $i$ turns the pair of cosine and sine into one complex number.
concepts.c:complex-number: The formula is an identity between powers of complex numbers.
concepts.c:trigonometric-function: Cosine and sine of the multiple angle $nx$ form the right side.
concepts.c:exponential-function: The exponential turns powers into multiples of the angle.

source.note: mathlib rewrites both sides with exp_mul_I ($\cos z + \sin z \cdot i = e^{zi}$) and the power rule exp_nat_mul.

proofs.name: Induction with angle addition
proofs.slogan: Multiply by $\cos x + i\sin x$ one factor at a time with the angle-addition formulas, then invert the factor for negative $n$.
proofs.scope: Steps 1 to 3 prove the case $n \ge 0$ by induction, and step 4 treats $n < 0$.

roles.why: The angle-addition formulas hold for the real angles $nx$ and $x$.
Induction covers $n \ge 0$, and inversion reduces $n < 0$ to the exponent $-n > 0$.

steps.slogan: Check the case $n = 0$, where both sides equal $1$.
steps.detail: The left side is the empty product $(\cos x + i\sin x)^0 = 1$. The right side is $\cos 0 + i\sin 0 = 1 + 0 = 1$.

steps.slogan: Multiply the case $n$ by $\cos x + i\sin x$ and expand with the angle-addition formulas.
steps.detail: The product $(\cos nx + i\sin nx)(\cos x + i\sin x)$ equals $(\cos nx\cos x - \sin nx\sin x) + i(\sin nx\cos x + \cos nx\sin x)$. The angle-addition formulas turn it into $\cos(n+1)x + i\sin(n+1)x$.

steps.slogan: Conclude the formula for all $n \ge 0$ by induction on $n$.
steps.detail: Step 1 is the base case and step 2 is the induction step, so $(\cos x + i\sin x)^n = \cos nx + i\sin nx$ for every natural number $n$.

steps.slogan: Invert $\cos x + i\sin x$ to reduce negative exponents to positive ones.
steps.detail: Since $(\cos x + i\sin x)(\cos x - i\sin x) = \cos^2 x + \sin^2 x = 1$, the inverse is $\cos(-x) + i\sin(-x)$. For $n = -m < 0$, step 3 with the angle $-x$ gives $(\cos x + i\sin x)^n = \cos(-mx) + i\sin(-mx) = \cos nx + i\sin nx$, which covers the remaining integers.

concepts.c:imaginary-unit: The imaginary unit $i$ turns the pair of cosine and sine into one complex number.
concepts.c:complex-number: The formula is an identity between powers of complex numbers.
concepts.c:trigonometric-function: Cosine and sine of the multiple angle $nx$ form the right side.

source.note: The classical induction proof from the angle-addition formulas of cosine and sine.
